name: C-beauty

card.summary: Chinese beauty products and trends, from skincare to makeup looks, that people borrow to refresh their routines and style.

quick.overview:
C-beauty is an umbrella term for contemporary beauty products, practices and ideals from China, spanning skincare, cosmetics, hair care and nail art. It often draws on traditional Chinese medicine and Chinese art [1].

People follow C-beauty for new product formats, quick innovation and makeup styles, and for routines like 'Morning C, Night A' for vitamins C and A serums [1]. It is a market and style trend, not a clinical treatment.
quick.how: Users buy products from Chinese brands such as Pechoin, HBN or Flower Knows, try gua sha and jade rollers, or copy Chinese-style makeup looks they see on social media [1].
quick.risks: As with any skincare, individual products may irritate skin. Wikipedia notes criticism of cultural appropriation around gua sha tools sold by non-Chinese brands [1].

lead: C-beauty (Chinese beauty) refers to beauty products, practices and ideals from China. China has the world's second-largest beauty market after the United States [1].

Brands include Pechoin (founded 1931, China's oldest skincare brand), HBN, Into You (credited with lip mud), Herborist, Kailijumei and Flower Knows [1]. The industry doubled its market share from 2017 to 2022, and domestic brands outsold international ones in China in 2022 [1].
Trends reaching global audiences include gua sha and jade rollers, which went viral on TikTok in 2021, and so-called Douyin makeup styles [1].

chain: Chinese skincare and makeup products and routines
Adopted for new textures, looks and routines
angle.text: People adopt C-beauty products and routines for skincare and makeup variety. Effects depend on the individual products.

paras: Products include cosmetics, skincare, hair care, perfumes and nail art. They are known for elaborate packaging, rapid innovation and cost-effectiveness, with some lines launching in three to six months [1].

The Guochao movement celebrates traditional Chinese culture in product design. K-beauty's popularity in China declined from 2018, which created room for domestic brands [1]. Content creators popularised 'Morning C, Night A' routines [1].
Since 2014 domestic cosmetics in China do not require animal testing if reliable safety reports are provided, and most imported general cosmetics have been exempt since May 2021 [1].

timeline.event: Gua sha and jade rollers go viral on TikTok [1]
